## Introduction

Stable angina, also referred to as typical angina or angina pectoris, or chronic stable angina, represents a symptom of myocardial ischemia. This condition manifests as chest discomfort or anginal equivalent symptoms that occur predictably and reproducibly with exertion or emotional stress and are relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Stable angina represents myocardial ischemia due to an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and demand, most commonly resulting from fixed atherosclerotic narrowing of the coronary arteries. Often, stable angina serves as one of the earliest clinical indicators or warning signs of underlying coronary artery disease. Unlike unstable angina or acute coronary syndromes, no plaque rupture or thrombosis is present, and myocardial necrosis does not occur.

Clinically, patients typically describe retrosternal pressure or heaviness that may radiate to the jaw, neck, shoulder, or left arm. The pain usually lasts a few minutes and resolves with rest or the use of nitrates. The pattern of symptoms is consistent over time, distinguishing it from unstable angina. Diagnosis is based on clinical history, supported by exercise stress testing, coronary imaging, or functional studies. Management includes lifestyle modification, pharmacologic therapy to reduce myocardial oxygen demand (eg, β-blockers, nitrates, calcium channel blockers), and risk factor control to prevent progression to acute coronary syndromes.

Approximately 11 million individuals in the United States experience angina. Recognizing its signs and symptoms remains crucial for a timely diagnosis and an appropriate clinical response. Effective risk stratification and management play a vital role in improving outcomes and preventing the progression of cardiovascular disease in this population.[1][2]

## Etiology

The mechanism behind stable angina is the result of a supply-demand mismatch. The myocardial oxygen demand transiently exceeds the myocardial oxygen supply, often leading to symptoms. The etiologies of stable angina include:

Coronary artery stenosis (fixed, the most common cause accounting for >90% cases)

Demand-supply mismatch (unrelated to coronary artery disease), eg, tachyarrhythmias, hypertension, aortic stenosis, left ventricular hypertrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, severe anemia/hypoxemia

Coronary artery vasospasm

Nonatherosclerotic coronary causes (eg, coronary artery congenital anomalies, a healed coronary artery dissection, an organized coronary embolus, postradiation, or vasculitis coronary changes) [3]

## Pathophysiology

Angina results from an imbalance between myocardial oxygen supply and myocardial oxygen demand. Gaining a clear understanding of the factors influencing each component remains essential for identifying and managing the underlying causes. Although coronary artery stenosis accounts for most cases of reduced supply, several other conditions, including coronary vasospasm, embolism, dissection, and microvascular disease, can also limit oxygen delivery to the myocardium.[3][7][8] Accurate diagnosis of angina requires a comprehensive clinical evaluation. Identifying the precise etiology enables effective medical optimization and targeted management of cardiovascular risk factors.

Atherosclerosis and Stable Angina

Atherosclerosis is the most common cause of stable angina. It begins with endothelial injury and dysfunction. Endothelial cells, which line the coronary arteries, play critical roles in regulating vascular tone and preventing intravascular thrombosis. Disruption in either of these functions contributes to the development of coronary heart disease. Various mechanisms, including stress, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, viral or bacterial infections, and immune complexes, can injure or impair the endothelial lining.

This injury triggers an immune response, leading to the formation of fibrous tissue. Subsequent smooth muscle remodeling and fibrous cap development may result in coronary artery stenosis or trigger acute coronary syndrome. Damaged endothelium causes increased permeability to lipoproteins and leukocyte adhesion. A loss of nitric oxide and prostacyclin occurs, which reduces vasodilation and enhances vasoconstriction and inflammation. Subsequent lipid entry, chronic inflammation, and smooth muscle cell migration result in the formation of a fibrofatty plaque that narrows the lumen.

This fixed obstruction limits maximal coronary flow (coronary flow reserve), so resting flow is normal, but flow during stress cannot increase sufficiently. Under increased myocardial oxygen demand, blood flow is inadequate; stenotic vessels fail to deliver sufficient oxygen to the myocardium, causing transient ischemia and initiating a reversible ischemic cascade. Four primary factors influence myocardial oxygen demand: heart rate, systolic blood pressure, myocardial wall tension, and contractility. Under normal circumstances, the body increases its oxygen supply to meet demand; however, this compensatory mechanism becomes insufficient when stenosis or other impairments are present.

Demand-Supply Mismatch and Stable Angina

Myocardial oxygen supply depends on the diameter and tone of the coronary arteries, collateral blood flow, perfusion pressure, and heart rate. During exercise, stress, tachycardia, or any condition that alters myocardial contractility or ventricular wall stress (preload, afterload), the fixed stenosis prevents an adequate increase in blood flow, resulting in transient myocardial ischemia.

Ishemia causes the release of adenosine, bradykinin, and lactate, which stimulate cardiac nociceptors (C fibers). These impulses travel via sympathetic afferents to spinal segments C7 to T4, perceived as retrosternal chest pain, possibly radiating to the arm, neck, or jaw. Since each spinal level corresponds with a specific dermatome, patients often describe discomfort in patterns that follow these dermatomal distributions.[9][10]

## History and Physical

Clinical History

Individuals with stable angina frequently present with a subacute rather than a chronic clinical pattern. Typical angina generally manifests as chest discomfort or an anginal equivalent that arises with exertion and resolves with rest or nitroglycerin. Anginal equivalents may include symptoms, eg, shortness of breath, nausea, or fatigue that appear disproportionate to the degree of physical activity.

Patients often describe typical angina as pressure-like, heavy, tight, or squeezing in nature. The discomfort usually involves a broad area of the chest rather than a specific localized point. Depending on the dermatomes involved, the pain may radiate to other regions.[11][12] Symptoms tend to intensify with increased myocardial demand during activities such as walking, lifting, or emotional stress.

Anginal episodes generally last between 2 and 5 minutes and typically subside with cessation of the triggering activity or administration of nitroglycerin.[13] Differentiating between cardiac and noncardiac chest pain requires a detailed analysis of symptoms. Key characteristics include the quality, location, precipitating and relieving factors, timing, and duration of the pain.[13] This clinical context helps distinguish anginal pain from other sources of pain.

Angina Risk Factors

History of pertinent risk factors includes:

Hypertension

Diabetes mellitus

Dyslipidemia

Smoking

Family history of premature CAD

Sedentary lifestyle or obesity

Age (men older than 45, women older than 55)

Physical Examination Findings

Physical examination is often normal at rest, as the ischemia is transient. However, evaluation during or immediately after exertion may reveal certain findings. Additionally, systemic findings suggesting risk factors or comorbidities can be identified, including:

Mildly anxious appearance

Pallor or diaphoresis (during attack)

Elevated blood pressure or tachycardia

S4 (atrial gallop) due to reduced left ventricular (LV) compliance during ischemia

S3 (if LV dysfunction present)

Xanthelasma, xanthomas (indicates hyperlipidemia)

Arcus senilis (indicates early-onset hyperlipidemia)

Diminished peripheral pulses in patients with peripheral arterial disease

Carotid bruit (atherosclerosis elsewhere)
